Sarah —

Appreciate the context and the model. Short answer: both approaches are common; we typically recommend a marginal structure for teams that want literal per-token incentives and a blended effective rate when customers prefer simpler, predictable line items. Below is a compact worked example using the bands you included. I attached the quick math in CSV too.

Worked example (monthly):
- Bands: 0–25M @ $0.020/token, 25–75M @ $0.016/token, 75M+ @ $0.013/token (marginal)
- If month = 90M tokens:
  - Marginal: (25M * 0.020) + (50M * 0.016) + (15M * 0.013) = $500k + $800k + $195k = $1,495,000 -> effective blended rate = $0.01661/token
  - Blended (tier hit at 75M): entire 90M * 0.013 = $1,170,000 -> effective blended = $0.01300/token

Key trade-offs:
- Marginal preserves a clearer per-token price signal and avoids sudden step-changes in billing when you cross a breakpoint.
- Blended is simpler on the invoice and allows for a steeper step-down (better for customers when they just step past a breakpoint).

Ratchet proposal (example language):
- If trailing 3-mo average > 120% of committed baseline for two consecutive quarters, Redwood reserves the right to move the customer to the next committed tier for the remainder of term (with a 30-day notice). Credits for prior overages can be applied as one-time adjustment.

Guardrails for bursting:
- Monthly invoice capped at 130% of baseline unless overage approved via written PO.
- True-up quarterly with marginal accounting so spikes are smoothed across the quarter.

Next steps: would you like a side-by-side line-item sample invoice for both methods for a 3-month simulated usage series? I can loop Priyom to add the implementation / billing mechanics.

Adding a couple of implementation notes from an ops and billing perspective so the procurement and engineering teams know what to expect: 

- Invoicing model: Redwood's billing engine supports both marginal and blended modes; marginal is default. Switching to blended is a configuration flag on the contract and will change how historical invoices are computed (we do not retroactively rebill).
- Metering: we use tokenized telemetry at request-level; for burst protection we can implement a configurable soft cap and an approval workflow (PO reference) to permit higher billed usage.
- Ratchet mechanics: recommend a 2-step ratchet to reduce churn risk — 1) provisional notice + 30 days to object and produce usage forecasts, 2) final ratchet effective at next invoice period. That gives you time to signal and adjust.

Operational example (quarterly smoothing):
- Compute monthly tokens, sum quarter, divide by 3 = quarter-average-month. Apply marginal pricing on quarter totals and then distribute the dollar totals back to monthly invoices proportionally. This avoids a single-month cliff.

I'll attach a short one-pager with suggested contract language for the ratchet and a diagram of the billing flow.
